COLLECTION 01

Ornamental Fish

Fish bring movement and colour to a composition. This family is presented as studies of form and finnage, with selection framed as questions to discuss rather than a stock list.

Prepare a fish enquiry
All collections

STUDIES

Colour and form, side by side.

Two illustrative studies. Descriptions note what is visible in the image; they are not confirmed species or available stock.

STUDY 01
Single-colour, long-finned form
Deep red throughout; the spread of the fins carries most of the visual weight.
STUDY 02
Banded, tall-bodied form
Vertical bands and long trailing fins read strongly against planted backgrounds.

SELECTION CONSIDERATIONS

What shapes a fish selection

Framed as questions for a conversation. Care requirements vary by fish and should be confirmed for each case.

i.

Colour and finnage

Is colour meant to lead the display or accent it? Long fins read beautifully in calm water but change how a fish fits with others.

ii.

Form and movement

Tall, slow-moving forms suit open water; small, quick fish bring life to planted edges. Movement is part of the composition.

iii.

Community fit

Which inhabitants are already there or planned? Temperament and pace matter as much as appearance.

iv.

Display context

Viewing distance, lighting and background colour all change how a fish is seen. A dark planted scape and a bright open tank ask for different choices.

Plants build depth and atmosphere. This family is organised around how foliage shapes a scape — layer, leaf form, colour and texture — not around a catalogue of species.

Prepare a plant enquiry

COMPOSITION

How plants shape an aquascape

Most planted displays read in three layers. Thinking in layers makes it easier to describe what a scape needs.

3
Background

Tall, upright growth that gives height and hides the back of the display.

2
Midground

Bushier forms that bridge the layers and soften hardscape edges.

1
Foreground

Low, fine growth that keeps the front open and creates a sense of depth.

3
2
1
Front view, simplified. Proportions are illustrative.
Illustrative study: red and bronze foliage against green.

VISUAL CHARACTERISTICS

What to look at in a plant
Leaf form
Broad leaves read as calm surfaces; fine leaves and stems read as texture and movement.
Colour
Most scapes are built on greens. A single group of red or bronze foliage becomes a focal point.
Texture
Mixing coarse and fine textures helps each layer stay distinct from a distance.
Growth habit
Upright, spreading or carpeting growth decides where a plant belongs in the layers.

Driftwood

Driftwood is the structure of a scape. Each piece is discussed by its lines, branching and mass, and by how its surface reads under water and light.

ROLE
The skeleton: lines, scale and the main direction of movement.
LOOK AT
Silhouette, branching, surface texture and tone.
Prepare a hardscape enquiry
All collections
Focal point
Open water
Main line
Simplified front view with thirds marked.

STRUCTURE

Structure sets the composition
Lines lead the eye

The main direction of a piece decides how a viewer moves through the display.

Mass sets the scale

A heavy base grounds the scene; fine branches make a display feel larger than it is.

Space lets it breathe

Leaving open water beside the structure gives fish room to be seen.

MATERIAL

Reading the material

Visual notes for choosing between pieces. Preparation and suitability depend on the individual piece and display, and should be confirmed case by case.

Silhouette
Seen from the main viewing side, does the outline have one clear direction or several competing ones?
Branching
Dense, fine branching creates detail and shelter; few heavy limbs create a bolder, calmer shape.
Surface
Deep grooves and worn edges catch light differently from smooth wood, and plants attach to them differently.
Tone
Warm brown tones contrast with green planting; darker wood recedes into a dark background.

h1: Bringing the beauty of nature a little further.
layouts.mainText:
OUR STORY

Bringing the beauty of nature a little further.

A proposed perspective for the Aquatic World brand: why living water matters, who it is for, and how it should be handled.

Illustrative waterfront scene. It does not depict company premises or a confirmed location.

I

Nature

Aplanted aquarium is a small landscape that keeps changing. Light moves through leaves, wood softens with time and fish settle into the spaces left for them. The brand begins from respect for that living quality — the idea that a display is grown and looked after, not simply assembled.

II

People

The people behind a beautiful display are rarely seen: the retailer who advises a first-time keeper, the aquascaper who spends weeks on a single layout, the enthusiast who rebuilds a tank until it feels right. Aquatic World is imagined as a partner to them — useful in conversation, careful in what it promises.

Good aquatic things travel far — when they are chosen with care.

III

Water

Water connects every part of the work, from the place a plant grows to the display where it finally sits. Moving living things through water asks for patience and honesty about what can and cannot be known in advance. That is where quality starts.

Still water. Slow decisions.

PROPOSED VALUES

What the brand would stand for

Draft values for discussion; they would need to be confirmed by a real organisation before public use.

Composition over collection

Help people build displays that work as a whole, not lists of items.

Care that can be explained

Every handling decision should have a reason someone can ask about.

Honesty about the unknown

Say clearly what is illustrative, uncertain or still to be confirmed.

layouts.title: Quality — Aquatic World
layouts.mainText:
QUALITY

A thoughtful selection process, explained.

Quality in living goods is mostly about decisions made before anything moves. This page sets out what a careful process should consider and the questions worth asking.

Proposed principles. Aquatic World is an illustrative concept. Nothing on this page is a certification, guarantee or audited standard.

THE PROCESS

Five considerations, in order

Each step pairs a principle with a question a buyer can reasonably ask.

01
Sourcing

Know where each item comes from and keep a record that can be shared.

ASK
Where does this come from, and how is that recorded?

02
Observation

Allow time to watch condition and behaviour before anything is offered.

ASK
How long is something observed before it is offered?

03
Preparation

Plan holding and acclimation around the receiving display, not a generic routine.

ASK
What do you need to know about my setup?

04
Handling & packing

Pack for the journey and the conditions, and keep handling to a minimum.

ASK
How is packing adapted to distance and timing?

05
Follow-up

Ask how things settled and record what should change next time.

ASK
What happens if something does not settle well?

Illustrative study image.

PRACTICAL QUESTIONS

Questions worth asking any supplier
What information comes with each item?
How are condition and behaviour checked?
How is packing chosen for distance and timing?
What should be ready before arrival?
Who can I talk to if something looks wrong?
What cannot be known in advance?

EXPECTATIONS

Reasonable expectations, on both sides
What a supplier can describe

How items are selected, observed, packed and followed up — and what records exist.

What depends on the receiver

A prepared display, a plan for arrival and honest information about the setup.

What no one can promise

Living things vary. Clear communication matters more than guarantees.

Have specific requirements?

Note them in an enquiry brief so they can be discussed first.

Discuss requirements
